Photograph: Ben Margot/AP US universities UC Berkeley professor admits to using AI to edit op-ed about students’ math skills Zvezdelina Stankova says she used AI to ‘help edit’ an article about some of her students being ‘five to eight years’ behind Sophie Sullivan Wed 19 Aug 2026 20.35 EDT Last modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 20.36 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A math professor at the University of California, Berkeley, criticizing a “severe” math deficiency among students in an op-ed for the San Francisco Standard , admitted to using artificial intelligence to help edit the piece. The Standard published a 2,000-word piece by Zvezdelina Stankova last week, in which the professor said some of her math students were “five to eight years” behind and lacked a “middle school” education on fractions and basic algebra. Stankova said the UC system’s test-blind admissions were to blame, suggesting that students who weren’t sufficiently prepared for the rigor of Berkeley’s mathematics program were admitted because a longstanding benchmark like the SAT had disappeared. Over the weekend, journalists at Berkeley’s student newspaper, the Daily Californian, noticed the op-ed’s language sounded like AI . According to Berkeley sophomore Francis Luo, they ran it through AI-detection software Pangram, which claimed 33% of the op-ed had been generated or assisted by AI. In response, Stankova admitted she had used AI software to “help edit the piece” but that the article was “the result of several hundred person-hours of intensive human work, of which about 80 hours are my own”. Stankova said by email she had used AI to locate “numerous documents and articles related to the initiative” but that “all analysis is the result of the team members”. When asked about their AI usage policy, the Standard – which published the op-ed – shared this statement by email: “While AI may assist, our expectation is that humans are behind every article we publish and take responsibility for every word. Our understanding in working with the author of this op ed was – and continues to be – that this piece reflects her and her colleagues’ extensive original analysis, research and expertise.” Stankova’s admission has prompted a larger debate on social media on the use of AI by academics. Some criticized Stankova, calling its use “ ironic ” for a piece discussing students’ underpreparedness, or arguing an op-ed should have been entirely original and written without artificial assistance. Others defended the professor, saying the use of AI was not a serious issue and distracted from the argument at hand. Stankova, in her email, said “the issue of how AI was used … is orthogonal to and a distraction from the thousands of hours our team has put into the initiative” of reinstating standardized tests in admission. The debate over whether tests like the SAT or ACT should be again used in UC admissions has intensified over recent years. In 2020, the UC regents voted to phase out the tests as a requirement for application; so did institutions like Harvard, Stanford, MIT and Yale. Each of those peer colleges have since reinstated the requirement. In her op-ed, Stankova shared data that she and her peers had analyzed, which suggested that the number of students with a “severe deficit” in their readiness for a calculus I class had tripled after test-blind admissions were introduced. Prior to publishing her op-ed last week, Stankova – in addition to more than 3,000 other UC faculty members – signed a June letter supporting admissions testing. Stankova, one of the letter’s authors, said AI was also used for editing there. The UC academic senate said in a late July statement that it would begin a review to determine whether standardized tests would again be used in admissions. If reinstated, the changes would affect fall 2028 admissions at earliest. The UC system also has its own “AI council”, which helps develop AI initiatives and resources for its colleges. Camille Crittenden, a member of the council, said she was unaware whether faculty had any specific guidance regarding the use of AI in personal research or editorials, but said that “most AI detection tools are still quite unreliable and lack nuance” with regard to Pangram. On its website, Pangram claims it correctly identifies AI-generated documents 99.66% of the time, or gives one false positive about every 24,000 documents scanned. Photograph: Guglielmo Mangiapane/Reuters Pope Leo XIV Pope Leo admitted to hospital for operation to remove growth on lung Leo arrived at hospital on Tuesday for the surgery, which is deemed low risk and could take place this afternoon Angela Giuffrida in Rome Tue 13 Oct 2026 07.27 EDT Last modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 07.28 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Pope Leo has been admitted to hospital in Rome for an operation to remove a small growth from his lung, a discovery a top Vatican cardinal said had come “like a bolt out of the blue”. In a rare moment of Vatican transparency, Leo, 71, said during his angelus prayer on Sunday that doctors had found a small nodule on his lung during a check-up , adding that it was “well-contained” and detected early. “The doctors believe it would be right to intervene and so, following their advice, I have decided to have the operation to remove it,” he said to the crowds gathered in St Peter’s Square. Leo, who in May last year became the first US-born leader of the Roman Catholic church, is being treated in Rome’s Gemelli hospital, where a large crowd greeted the pontiff. The Vatican has not disclosed the timing of the operation, although it could take place on Tuesday afternoon, according to Italian media reports. All of his appointments have been cancelled until 20 October. Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, said he had seen Leo on Monday night. “We spoke with great serenity,” Parolin told Rai News . “He is truly a great example. The announcement came like a bolt out of the blue, nobody expected it. Thank God it was detected immediately, so the operation could take place immediately. Normally, when these things are caught in time, they can be resolved.” The operation is deemed low risk and will determine whether the nodule is malignant. Leo will stay in the 10-floor private-patient wing but not in the papal suite, which is being renovated. The Chicago-born pope, who enjoys sports, especially playing tennis, is generally believed to be in good health. He often makes use of the papal retreat in Castel Gandolfo, close to Rome. Leo travelled to France on a papal visit in September and is scheduled to go to South America in November for a 12-day trip covering 10 cities. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day after newsletter promotion The weekly papal audience on Wednesday will be led by Luis Antonio Tagle, a cardinal from the Philippines who last week was elected dean of the college of cardinals – the authority that presides over papal conclaves. The Gemelli, located in the north-west of the Italian capital, is renowned for treating reigning popes. Pope John Paul II stayed there so many times that the Vatican worked with the hospital to establish the high security papal suite. Leo’s predecessor, Francis, spent more than five weeks in the hospital, being treated for bronchitis which developed into bilateral pneumonia. He died at home in Casa Santa Marta in Vatican City on 21 April 2025, just under a month after being discharged. Photograph: Lukas Coch/EPA Anthony Albanese Anthony Albanese apologises for hot-mic gaffe after Coalition criticises ‘locker-room talk’ Prime minister says he and Chris Bowen were having ‘light-hearted banter’ when they were caught discussing where they keep their phones Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast Tom McIlroy in Manila Sat 14 Nov 2026 22.49 EST Last modified on Sat 14 Nov 2026 22.59 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Anthony Albanese has apologised for a hot-mic gaffe at the UN climate talks in Turkey, saying he regretted being overheard discussing mobile phone radiation and “dicks” in a candid conversation. “I of course regret that. I apologise,” Albanese said during a visit to the Australian warship HMAS Stalwart in the Philippines on Sunday. “This was a private conversation, we thought, between two friends having a bit of light-hearted banter.” Ahead of a meeting at the Cop31 climate summit in Antalya on Friday, Albanese and the climate change minister, Chris Bowen , were caught on camera discussing which pocket they use to keep their mobile phone. Albanese can be heard telling Bowen that he should store his phone away from his heart because “it can interfere with your rhythm”. Laughing, Bowen asks whether the advice was because a phone can be “a little bit radioactive”. Albanese says “it makes absolute sense”, before Bowen replies that he was more conscious of putting his phone in his pants pocket. The prime minister asks: “Because of your dick?” Bowen agrees and says: “Arguably more important than the heart.” On Sunday, Albanese played down the incident which occurred ahead of a meeting with business leaders in Antalya. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here “No one was hurt or harmed. We weren’t having private banter which criticised anyone,” he said. The speedy apology is in contrast to previous gaffes by Albanese, including long-running controversy over comments about the gift of melons from Japan’s prime minister , Sanae Takaichi, on a podcast. Albanese previously apologised for saying he would “shag” Australian singer Kylie Minogue in the same episode of the Bush Deep podcast. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Politics, really Our political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for you after newsletter promotion Anthony Albanese’s coffee diplomacy can’t remove shadow of domestic politics at Cop31 Read more The melons comment risked becoming an international incident, as Albanese repeatedly insisted the comments and his corresponding hand gestures were not a reference to breasts. Japan’s government sent a diplomatic cable to Australia in July, days after the podcast originally aired, claiming there had been “sensationalised reporting in the Australian media” and saying they detected no “ill intention” in Albanese’s statement. The Coalition on Sunday criticised Albanese and Bowen’s comments. Opposition frontbencher James Paterson said the remarks were unfortunate, telling News24 they could damage impressions of Australia on the world stage. “That locker-room talk like that has a time and a place and it’s not at international summits when you’re the prime minister of Australia talking to your energy minister,” he said. But the employment minister, Amanda Rishworth, dismissed the criticism, saying the comments were a joke. “This is a private conversation in between meetings,” she said. “I know that a hot-mic incident is very exciting for people ... but really, there are bigger issues to tackle and discuss.” Earlier a spokesperson for the prime minister said the hot-mic comments were “a joke in between meetings”. Albanese is in the Philippines for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit and high-level diplomatic meetings, including with the US president, Donald Trump. He will hold formal bilateral talks with the Filipino president, Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr, on Sunday and visited a Jollibee fast food restaurant to celebrate the chain’s expansion to Australia.
